title: Fixed, variable, direct & indirect costs
blurb: Classify any project cost as fixed or variable and as direct or indirect, tell capital from operational costs, and explain why it matters.
question: A housing association is replacing 200 kitchens. Its budget includes kitchen units for each home, fitters paid by the hour, a one-off licence for scheduling software, and a share of head-office HR and finance costs. How should each cost be classified, and why does the project manager need to know?

teach.h: Two separate questions about every cost
teach.body: Every project cost can be classified in two independent ways. First, how does it BEHAVE? A fixed cost does not change with the amount of work done; a variable cost rises and falls with the quantity of work or hours. Second, can it be TRACED to the project? A direct cost is attributable to this project; an indirect cost is a shared overhead apportioned across the organisation's work. Knowing both is how a budget becomes complete and controllable.

teach.caption: Behaviour (rows) and traceability (columns) are different questions, so any combination is possible.

rows.label: Examples
values: Licence fee, set-up fee, fixed design fee
Materials, hourly labour, printing per copy

rows.label: Risk to watch
values: Time-based fixed costs keep running if late
Overtime or extra quantities push it up

teach.h: Total cost = fixed part + variable part
teach.caption: Illustrative: £40k fixed costs are paid whatever happens; each kitchen then adds about £4k of variable cost.

rows.label: How it gets in the budget

teach.caption: Overheads is the everyday word for indirect costs.

teach.body: Leave out indirect costs and the true cost of the project is understated, so the business case looks better than it is. Separating fixed from variable shows what drives cost: if the quantity of work grows or the team works overtime, variable costs climb, while a delay keeps time-based fixed costs such as site hire running. It also tells the PM where control lies: direct costs are the PM's to manage, while indirect allocations are normally set by finance.

rows.label: At handover
values: Asset moves to the asset register

teach.caption: The organisation's finance function sets the exact rules for what counts as capital.

teach.text: Exam trap: 'direct' does not mean 'variable', and 'indirect' does not mean 'fixed'. They answer different questions. A contractor paid by the hour to build a deliverable is direct AND variable; a one-off licence bought just for the project is direct AND fixed.

teach.body: Kitchen units and fitters' hourly pay are direct and variable: fit more kitchens or work overtime and they rise. The scheduling-software licence is direct and fixed: one fee whatever the number of homes. The share of head-office HR and finance is indirect: it supports many projects and is apportioned by finance. The new kitchens are capital; the tenants' repair service afterwards is an operational cost that BAU will carry.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define each type in one line: fixed (doesn't vary with work done), variable (varies with quantity or hours), direct (attributable to the project), indirect (shared overhead).
Give a project example of each, ideally from the scenario in the question.
Explain that behaviour and traceability are separate, so a cost has one label from each pair.
Say why it matters: complete budget (indirects included), understanding cost drivers, knowing what the PM controls.
If asked, add capital (asset) versus operational (running) costs and the handover of running costs to BAU.
Fixed: same whatever the amount of work. Variable: moves with quantity or hours.
Direct: traceable to the project. Indirect: shared overheads apportioned to it.
Every cost gets one label from each pair, for example direct and variable.
Omitting indirect costs understates the true cost of the project.
Capital buys lasting assets; operational costs run the business and pass to BAU.

summary: You can now classify any project cost by behaviour (fixed or variable) and traceability (direct or indirect), and tell capital from operational costs. You can also explain why each distinction matters for a complete budget and for cost control.

A.q: A construction project pays for concrete by the cubic metre, and the amount needed varies from phase to phase. How is this cost best described?
A.why: The cost rises and falls with the quantity used, which is the definition of a variable cost.

whyNot.0: A fixed cost would stay the same however much concrete was used.
whyNot.1: Concrete for the project is clearly traceable to it, so it is direct, not indirect.
whyNot.3: Capital reserve is not a cost behaviour; the question is about how the cost varies.

A.q: Which of the following is the best example of an INDIRECT cost to a project?
options: Hire of a crane used only on this site
A share of the head-office finance team
Wages of the engineers building the bridge
Steel bought for the project's structure
A.why: The finance team supports the whole organisation, so its cost can't be traced to one project and is apportioned as an overhead.

whyNot.0: A crane used only on this site is attributable to the project, so it is direct.
whyNot.2: Engineers building the deliverable are a direct labour cost.
whyNot.3: Steel for the project's structure is a direct materials cost.

A.q: Complete the statement: a fixed cost is one that…
options: stays the same whatever the amount of work done
can always be traced to a single work package
is paid from the organisation's capital budget
rises steadily as more of the work is completed
A.why: Fixed describes behaviour: the cost does not change with the level of activity or output, such as a one-off licence fee.

whyNot.1: Being traceable to the work describes a direct cost, which is a different question.
whyNot.2: Capital versus operational is a separate classification from fixed versus variable.
whyNot.3: A cost that rises with work done is variable.

B.q: Specialist consultants are paid an hourly rate for time spent on the project's own deliverables. How should their cost be classified?
B.why: Their cost moves with hours worked (variable) and is attributable to the project's deliverables (direct).

whyNot.0: Hourly pay is not fixed, and work on the project's deliverables is traceable to it.
whyNot.1: Hourly pay rises with hours worked, so it is variable, not fixed.
whyNot.2: The work is on the project's own deliverables, so it is direct, not an overhead.

B.q: A budget omits the project's share of shared organisational overheads. What is the MOST likely consequence?
options: The fixed costs will be recorded twice
The true cost of the project is understated
The schedule will need to be re-sequenced
Variable costs will fall as work increases
B.why: Indirect costs are real costs of doing the project; leaving them out understates its true cost, flattering the business case and risking overruns.

whyNot.0: Omitting overheads leaves something out; it doesn't double count anything.
whyNot.2: Overhead allocation is a cost matter and doesn't change the activity sequence.
whyNot.3: Variable costs rise with work, and this has nothing to do with omitted overheads.

B.q: A project buys new servers that will be used for years after the project ends, and also pays an annual support subscription for them. Which statement is correct?
B.why: The servers are a lasting asset, so they are capital; the support subscription is a recurring running cost, so it is operational and will usually pass to BAU after handover.

whyNot.0: The servers are an asset with a life of several years, which is what capital spend buys.
whyNot.1: An annual subscription is a running cost of operating the asset, not an asset itself.
whyNot.3: This reverses them: the asset is capital and the recurring support is operational.

C.q: On a kitchen replacement project, fixed costs are unchanged this month but variable costs have risen sharply. Which is the MOST likely cause?
options: More kitchens were fitted than planned
The sponsor approved the business case
C.why: Variable costs move with the quantity of work done, so fitting more kitchens (more units, more fitter hours) raises them while fixed costs stay put.

whyNot.0: A licence fee is a fixed cost, and fixed costs were unchanged.
whyNot.2: Re-apportioning rent changes an indirect allocation, not variable costs.
whyNot.3: Approving the business case doesn't itself change the cost of work done.

C.q: Which is NOT a good reason for a project manager to separate direct from indirect costs?
options: To show which costs the PM can directly control
To make sure overheads are not left out
To assign costs to the right work packages
To make the project look cheaper to the board
C.why: Classification is about accuracy and control. Using it to present a lower cost than reality would undermine the business case and governance.

whyNot.0: This is a valid reason: direct costs are the PM's to manage, indirect allocations usually aren't.
whyNot.1: This is a valid reason: identifying indirect costs makes the budget complete.
whyNot.2: This is a valid reason: direct costs are assigned to the work packages that cause them.

C.q: An iterative software project uses the same dedicated team in every two-week time box. How does the team's cost MOST likely behave per time box?
options: As an indirect overhead of the business
As a cost that falls each time box
As capital that never needs reporting
C.why: A stable team costs much the same each time box, which is why iterative projects fix time and cost per time box and let scope flex instead.

whyNot.1: The team works on the project's own deliverables, so its cost is direct.
whyNot.2: With the same people and length of time box, cost per time box stays about the same, not falling.
whyNot.3: All project costs must be reported, whatever their classification.

reteach.title: Running a market stall
reteach.question: Imagine you run a burger stall at a summer festival. Which of your costs are fixed, which are variable, and which are really someone else's shared costs?

blocks.h: Pitch fee, buns and the organiser's toilets
blocks.body: Your pitch fee is the same whether you sell 10 burgers or 1,000: fixed. Buns, burgers and napkins rise with every sale: variable. Both are direct, because they are clearly for your stall. The festival's security, toilets and cleaning serve every trader, so the organiser shares that cost out in everyone's fees: that is an indirect cost, an overhead. Your new griddle, which you'll use for years, is capital; the gas you burn each day is operational.

blocks.text: Two questions, two labels: 'Does it change with sales?' gives fixed or variable. 'Is it just for my stall?' gives direct or indirect.

explain.body: A fixed cost does not change with the amount of work done: a licence fee, a set-up fee or a fixed design fee. Watch time-based fixed costs, such as monthly site hire: they don't vary with output, but they keep running if the project is late.

test.q: Which of these is the clearest example of a fixed project cost?
test.why: A one-off licence fee costs the same however much work is done, so it is fixed.

whyNot.0: Materials bought per unit rise with quantity: variable.
whyNot.2: Overtime rises with hours worked: variable.
whyNot.3: Fuel use rises with how much the vehicles work: variable.

explain.body: A variable cost rises and falls with the quantity of work or hours: materials, hourly labour, printing per copy. They are controlled by managing quantities, rates and hours, so extra scope or overtime shows up here first.

test.q: The sponsor asks the team to work extra paid hours for six weeks. Which cost type will this most likely increase?
test.why: Paid hours scale with time worked, so extra hours raise variable labour costs.

whyNot.0: The extra hours are for this project's work, so they are not shared overheads.
whyNot.1: Fixed costs don't change with hours worked.
whyNot.2: Extra working hours don't buy a lasting asset.

explain.body: Direct costs can be attributed to the project (its team, equipment and materials). Indirect costs, or overheads, support many activities (office space, IT, HR, admin) and are apportioned to projects using an agreed rule, usually set by finance.

test.q: What is the key difference between direct and indirect costs?
options: Whether the cost is paid monthly
Whether the cost is over budget
Whether the cost is for an asset
test.why: Direct costs can be specifically identified with the project; indirect costs are shared and must be apportioned.

whyNot.1: Payment frequency doesn't decide whether a cost is direct.
whyNot.2: Performance against budget is a separate matter from classification.
whyNot.3: Whether a cost buys an asset is the capital versus operational question.

explain.body: Capital spend creates or buys a lasting asset (a building, equipment, a new system). Operational spend keeps the business running (maintenance, support, subscriptions). At closure, assets go onto the organisation's records and running costs pass to the BAU budget.

test.q: Who normally pays the ongoing running costs of a new system once the project has handed it over?
test.why: Running a delivered system is an operational cost of the business, so it moves to the BAU operating budget at handover.

whyNot.0: Contingency is for project risks and is released when the project closes.
whyNot.1: A warranty covers defects for a period; it doesn't fund everyday running.
whyNot.3: The project's capital budget closes with the project and funds the asset, not its running.
